extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (particularly Kantian teleology and the philosophy of biology)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and apply Kant's account of purposiveness, distinguishing determinant vs reflective judgement, the limits of dogmatic proof for natural purposes, and the roles of competing systems (Epicureanism, Spinozism, Hylozoism, Theism) in explaining purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epicurean mechanism denies intentionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Epicurus’s system explains purposive appearance by blind chance and mechanical laws, denying intentionality and the distinction between a Technic of nature and mere mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an account treats agreement of developed products with our concepts of purpose as accidental; it explains neither true purposiveness nor the illusion in teleological judgements, and therefore fails to establish Idealism of purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spinozistic fatalism removes design and contingency
rubrics_metrics.description: Spinoza reduces purposiveness to accidents inhering in a single original Being and denies that the original Being acts through Understanding or design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While securing ontological unity necessary for purposiveness, this view eliminates contingency and design; unity of subject does not constitute a unity of purpose, so Spinozism cannot account for purposive reference as requiring an understanding or design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hylozoism bases purposiveness in life of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Realism rooted in a physical ground (hylozoism) locates purposiveness in the life of matter or a world-soul—analogy to a faculty acting with design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The possibility of living matter cannot be established a priori; using life of matter to explain purposiveness is circular because we know such life only through organized beings, so hylozoism fails to furnish a non-question-begging explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theism attributes purposiveness to an intelligent original cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Realism rooted in a hyperphysical ground (theism) derives purposiveness from an intelligent original Being that produces natural ends by design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although superior in rescuing purposiveness from Idealism, theism cannot be dogmatically proved for the determinant Judgement; it provides at best a reflective-ground explanation and does not yield objective certainty about nature's origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for dogmatic treatment: objective reality for determinant judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat the concept of a natural purpose dogmatically (i.e., constitutively for the determinant Judgement) one must establish its objective reality—show that objects conforming to the concept are possible independent of our faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without objective reality the concept cannot validly subsume natural things under it; otherwise all synthetic predicates about purposes remain merely problematical, not constitutive of objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendence of the concept of natural purpose for determinant judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of a thing as a natural purpose is transcendent for the determinant Judgement because it combines natural necessity with contingency and requires reference to a supersensible ground not derivable from experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it cannot be derived from experience nor is required for its possibility, its objective reality cannot be assured; thus it cannot serve as a constitutive principle for determining objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness as a regulative (critical) principle for reflective judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of objective purposiveness of nature functions as a critical (regulative) principle of Reason for the reflective Judgement, guiding investigation without asserting constitutive claims about objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is a necessary maxim for studying organized products: useful and often indispensable for empirical investigation of organisms, but it only prescribes how we must use our cognitive faculties (subjectively), not what the Object is objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical methodological maxim: ascribe design when investigating organized products
rubrics_metrics.description: For empirical inquiry into organized beings we are indispensably obliged to ascribe design to nature as a guiding maxim of reflective judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim helps discover laws concealed by limited insight into mechanism; it is useful and necessary for studying many natural products, though not constitutive for claims about nature as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology cannot dogmatically prove God's existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological argument shows only that, given the constitution of our cognitive faculties, we cannot think the possibility of many organized natural products except by representing a designing supreme cause; it does not amount to an objective proof that such a Being exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best permissible formula is subjective: we cannot otherwise make comprehensible purposiveness than by representing the world as product of an intelligent cause. This suffices for human reflective use but not for dogmatic, determinant proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between dogmatic (constitutive) and critical (regulative) use of concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Dogmatic use subsumes concepts under higher principles to determine objects (constitutive); critical use considers concepts relative to our cognitive faculties (regulative) without claiming objective determination of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the Understanding cannot provide constitutive concepts, Reason supplies regulative Ideas that guide inquiry but are limited in objective validity to the subject's point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-specific distinction: possibility vs actuality affects judgement validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Human understanding distinguishes possibility (representation in thought) from actuality (intuition/given), a distinction that has merely subjective validity for human cognition and affects how concepts can be taken as proof of actuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subjective distinction makes certain Ideas indispensable as regulative principles for human Reason while preventing them from serving as constitutive proofs about objects or higher beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peculiarity of human (discursive) Understanding causes representation of natural products as purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because human Understanding is discursive—proceeding from universal concepts to particulars and not determining the particular—it represents certain natural products as if produced according to purpose to account for contingent conformity to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contingency of how particulars accord with universals leads us to think of an organising representation (a whole whose representation grounds the possibility of its parts)—this representational move is what makes the concept of purpose arise for human Judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast with hypothetical intuitive Understanding (whole-to-parts) removes need for purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: An intuitive Understanding that proceeds synthetically from whole to parts would not face contingency between universal and particular and so would not need to represent natural products as purposive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant uses this contrast to show purposiveness arises from our specific cognitive constitution (discursive understanding), not necessarily from nature itself; thus purposiveness is a feature of judgement, not proven ontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: purposiveness is necessary for reflective but not determinant judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Purposiveness is necessary as a subjective maxim for human reflective judgement (especially in biology), but it does not determine objects constitutively for determinant judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence one must not convert regulative teleological principles into dogmatic assertions about nature; their legitimacy lies in guiding empirical inquiry and making organized phenomena comprehensible to human cognition.
